Eris. A dwarf planet in the outer solar system, slightly more distant and marginally more massive than Pluto. Its discovery in 2005 by Mike Brown's team at Caltech triggered the International Astronomical Union's 2006 reclassification that demoted Pluto and created the dwarf-planet category.

Eris was discovered on January 5th, 2005 by Mike Brown, Chad Trujillo, and David Rabinowitz. The team initially designated it a tenth planet, sparking a reclassification crisis. Eris is more massive than Pluto — its mass is roughly 27.8 times 10 to the 20 kilograms, compared to Pluto's 13 times 10 to the 20 kilograms. This discovery argued that Pluto could not hold unique status, forcing the definition question.

The planet was named for the Greek goddess of discord, fitting given its role in sparking the planetary redefinition controversy. Eris has an extreme orbit. Its semi-major axis is roughly 96 astronomical units, with a perihelion of about 38 astronomical units — that's inside Pluto's orbit — and an aphelion of roughly 98 astronomical units. Its orbital eccentricity of 0.44 is the highest of any known dwarf planet.

Eris has one known moon, Dysnomia, the goddess of lawlessness, discovered in 2005. It orbits at roughly 37,350 kilometers distance and has been used to refine Eris's mass through orbital mechanics. The planet's surface is remarkably reflective, among the brightest known solar-system bodies per unit area. It's likely covered in frozen methane, nitrogen, or ethane, with an albedo of about 0.96.

Unlike Kuiper Belt bodies in stable orbits, Eris resides in the scattered disk beyond the Belt. It and others like it were scattered outward by early solar-system gravitational chaos, leaving low-density, high-eccentricity orbits. Eris shares origins and dynamics with Kuiper Belt bodies and stands as the archetype of the icy outer dwarf-planet population, a direct rival to Pluto in defining the dwarf-planet category.
